item.research_question: How does temperature influence the transition between smooth (mild) and intermittent (wild) plastic flow in body-centered cubic (bcc) Niobium, and what is the underlying dislocation mechanism governing this bimodal behavior?
item.material_system: Single-crystal Niobium (Nb), commercially pure, oriented along the ⟨123⟩ direction
item.processing_route: Focused ion beam (FIB) milling to fabricate cylindrical microcrystals (height 6 μm, diameter 2 μm); uniaxial microcompression testing at a displacement rate of 0.6 nm s⁻¹ (strain rate 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹) across temperatures of 173–368 K; 3D discrete dislocation dynamics (DDD) simulations using the MODELib package at strain rates of 718 s⁻¹ and 7180 s⁻¹
item.test_conditions: Temperatures: 173 K, 263 K, 298 K, 323 K, 368 K; Strain rates: 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ (experiment), 718 s⁻¹ and 7180 s⁻¹ (simulation); Loading axis: ⟨123⟩; Slip system: {211}⟨111⟩
key_findings: Plasticity is bimodal, consisting of thermally activated smooth flow ('mild') and athermal intermittent bursts ('wild') that coexist across the temperature regime.
The effective barrier energy for athermal dislocation avalanches is 0.04 eV, which is an order of magnitude smaller than the 0.3 eV barrier energy for smooth plastic flow at 298 K.
The distribution of avalanche sizes shifts from a scale-free power law at 298–368 K to an exponential (Weibull) distribution at 173 K, with a characteristic length scale of ~0.3 nm.
The fraction of athermal slip activity (η) increases markedly at the critical temperature Tc (approx. 290–320 K), where screw and edge dislocation mobilities equalize.
DDD simulations confirm that screw dislocations are the dominant segment type (>90%) in avalanches, despite the observed athermal behavior.
Screw dislocations involved in avalanches are subjected to local stresses significantly exceeding the Peierls stress (τ > τP), neutralizing their thermal sensitivity.
The proportion of athermal strain contribution decreases with decreasing temperature due to a reduction in the effective screening length for elastic coupling.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that athermal screw dislocation slip is driven by the emergence of local stresses in screw dislocation pileups that exceed the Peierls stress (τP). When τ > τP, screw dislocations exhibit viscous motion similar to edge dislocations, effectively bypassing the classical thermally activated kink-pair nucleation mechanism. As temperature decreases, the Peierls potential increases, reducing the 'screening distance' (2d0) for elastic coupling between dislocations, which suppresses the length scale of avalanches and transitions the statistics from scale-free to exponential.
item.limitations: The experimental sensor resolution limits the ability to detect rearrangements smaller than the current noise threshold (~0.165 nm), preventing observation of potential single-armed spiral source activity at very low temperatures. Additionally, the DDD simulations were performed at strain rates (718 s⁻¹) much higher than experimental rates (10⁻⁴ s⁻¹), though the authors note the strain-rate sensitivity exponents match.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that verifying the activity of single-armed spiral sources at very low temperatures would require nanomechanical testing with displacement resolution higher than current state-of-the-art capabilities. They also propose that the ratio of athermal to total plastic strain (η) could serve as a direct experimental method to determine the critical temperature Tc.
quotes: Plasticity is shown to be bimodal across the studied temperature regime, with conventional thermally-activated smooth plastic flow ('mild') coexisting with sporadic bursts ('wild') controlled by athermal screw dislocation activity.
This is clearly an order of magnitude smaller than that obtained from the averaging of the smooth stress–strain segments and also the classical barrier energies of bulk crystals.
Above τP screw dislocations display a viscous motion much in the manner of their edge counterparts, i.e., non-thermally activated.
